title: Learning a Musical Instrument
description: Four recordings about learning an instrument: a guitar teacher interview, a family chat about drums, a practice talk and a concert announcement.
instructions: Read the questions for each part first. Then press Play and listen. Choose the best answer (A, B or C) for each question.

parts.title: Part 1 · A guitar teacher
parts.intro: You will hear a radio presenter, Rita, interviewing a guitar teacher, Joe.

script.speaker: Rita
script.text: Today on Music Matters, I'm talking to Joe Morgan, who has taught guitar for fifteen years. Joe, what's the biggest mistake beginners make?

script.speaker: Joe
script.text: Trying to learn too fast. They practise for three hours on Saturday, and then nothing for the rest of the week. Twenty minutes every day is far better.

script.speaker: Rita
script.text: Is it true that you need to start as a child?

script.speaker: Joe
script.text: That's a myth. Children learn quickly, but adults have an advantage, too. They understand why they're practising, and they're more patient. My oldest student started at seventy-two.

script.speaker: Rita
script.text: That's wonderful. Is the guitar a good first instrument?

script.speaker: Joe
script.text: It's popular because you can play a simple song after a few weeks. But the first month is hard, because your fingers hurt. Many people give up at that point.

script.speaker: Rita
script.text: What should they do?

script.speaker: Joe
script.text: Keep going. After about two weeks, your fingertips become hard, and it stops hurting. I always tell students that pain is temporary.

script.speaker: Rita
script.text: Should they buy an expensive guitar?

script.speaker: Joe
script.text: Definitely not. A cheap guitar in good condition is fine. I advise renting for the first three months, until you're sure you enjoy it.

parts.title: Part 2 · Mother and son
parts.intro: You will hear a teenager, Nam, talking to his mother, Mai, about learning an instrument.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: Mum, can I ask you something? I'd like to learn the drums.

script.speaker: Mai
script.text: The drums? In this flat? The neighbours would go mad. Why not the piano? We have the keyboard in the cupboard.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: The keyboard is boring. Everyone at school plays piano. I want something different.

script.speaker: Mai
script.text: I see. But drums are loud, and they're expensive. A good set costs about four hundred pounds.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: I've been saving. I have one hundred and fifty pounds from my birthday and my weekend job. And there are electronic drums with headphones, so nobody hears them.

script.speaker: Mai
script.text: Hmm, that's clever. Where did you learn this?

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: My friend Jack has a set. He says the lessons at the music centre are only fifteen pounds for half an hour.

script.speaker: Mai
script.text: That's cheaper than I thought. Let's make a deal. If you take lessons for three months and practise every day, I'll pay half of the drum kit.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: Seriously? Thanks, Mum! You're the best.

script.speaker: Mai
script.text: Don't thank me yet. If I hear you playing at midnight, the deal is off.

parts.title: Part 3 · Advice about practice
parts.intro: You will hear the director of a music school, Mr Clarke, giving advice to parents and students.

script.speaker: Mr Clarke
script.text: Good evening, parents and students, and welcome to the Greenfield Music School. I'm Mr Clarke, the director. I'd like to give you some advice about practice, because it's the question I'm asked most often.

script.speaker: Mr Clarke
script.text: First, choose a regular time. Many families find that before dinner works well, because children are not too tired or too hungry. Whatever you choose, make it part of the daily routine, like brushing your teeth.

script.speaker: Mr Clarke
script.text: Second, short sessions are better than long ones. For beginners under ten, fifteen minutes is enough. Older students may do thirty to forty-five minutes. If you practise for an hour but you're thinking about something else, it's wasted time.

script.speaker: Mr Clarke
script.text: Third, always start with something easy. A piece you already know well makes you feel good, and a good mood helps you work on the difficult parts.

script.speaker: Mr Clarke
script.text: Fourth, record yourself on your phone. Listening to your own playing is uncomfortable at first, but it's the quickest way to improve. You'll hear mistakes that you can't notice while you're playing.

script.speaker: Mr Clarke
script.text: Parents, please don't sit beside your child and correct every note. That makes practice stressful. Instead, ask them to play you a piece, and say what you enjoyed about it.

script.speaker: Mr Clarke
script.text: Finally, be patient. Progress isn't a straight line. Some weeks you'll feel stuck, and then suddenly everything becomes easier.

parts.title: Part 4 · The end of term concert
parts.intro: You will hear a message from Ms Hill of the Greenfield Music School.

script.speaker: Ms Hill
script.text: Hello, this is Ms Hill from the Greenfield Music School with an important message about our end of term concert.

script.speaker: Ms Hill
script.text: The concert will take place on Friday the sixth of December at seven o'clock in the school hall. The doors open at half past six.

script.speaker: Ms Hill
script.text: Every student will play one piece, so the concert will last about two hours. Students should arrive at six o'clock to warm up. Please bring your own music stand and a bottle of water.

script.speaker: Ms Hill
script.text: The order of performance will be on the notice board from Monday. Younger students will play first, and the guitar group will close the programme.

script.speaker: Ms Hill
script.text: Tickets are free, but each family is limited to four, because the hall has only two hundred seats. You can collect them from the office until Wednesday.

script.speaker: Ms Hill
script.text: Please remember that you cannot take photographs during the performances, because the flash upsets the players. After the concert, there will be juice and cakes in the foyer, and you can take as many photographs as you like.

script.speaker: Ms Hill
script.text: If a student is ill and cannot play, please phone the office before Thursday, so that we can change the programme. Thank you, and good luck to everyone.

They start too late
They try to learn too fast

Three hours at the weekend
Twenty minutes every day
